हो ची मिन्ह सिटी और दक्षिणी क्षेत्र में जल्द ही बारिश का मौसम समाप्त हो जाएगा, और अल नीनो के चरम पर पहुंचने के साथ ही भीषण गर्मी पड़ सकती है।
भविष्यवाणी की गई है कि 2026-2027 का अल नीनो अत्यधिक तीव्र तीव्रता तक पहुंचेगा, जिससे दक्षिणी वियतनाम में वर्षा ऋतु समय से पहले समाप्त हो जाएगी, जिसके परिणामस्वरूप भीषण गर्मी, सूखा और खारे पानी के गंभीर घुसपैठ का खतरा पैदा हो जाएगा।
VietNamNet•05/09/2026
अल नीनो का चरम 2026 के अंत या 2027 की शुरुआत में हो सकता है।
दक्षिणी वियतनाम जल मौसम विज्ञान स्टेशन के जल मौसम विज्ञान पूर्वानुमान विभाग की मौसम पूर्वानुमानकर्ता किउ थी थुई ने पिछले 70 वर्षों में अल नीनो की घटनाओं से संबंधित आंकड़े जारी किए हैं, साथ ही इस घटना से प्रभावित वर्षों के दौरान दक्षिणी वियतनाम की मौसम विशेषताओं का विवरण भी दिया है।
इसके अतिरिक्त, मौसम पूर्वानुमानकर्ता ने 2026 के अंत और 2027 की शुरुआत के दौरान दक्षिणी वियतनाम में मौसम के विकास का आकलन भी प्रदान किया।
लगभग एक सदी तक फैले जलवायु डेटा श्रृंखला के विश्लेषण के अनुसार, इतिहास में सबसे शक्तिशाली अल नीनो घटनाएं 1982-1983, 1997-1998 और 2015-2016 की अवधि के दौरान हुईं।
इसी प्रकार, पूर्वानुमान डेटा से पता चलता है कि 2026-2027 के अल नीनो का चक्र और तीव्रता उपर्युक्त रिकॉर्ड तोड़ने वाली अल नीनो घटनाओं के समान होगी।
मौसम पूर्वानुमानकर्ता किउ थी थूई ने कहा, "यह अनुमान लगाया गया है कि अल नीनो की तीव्रता 2026 के अंत से 2027 की शुरुआत तक चरम पर होगी, जिसके बाद धीरे-धीरे कम हो जाएगी। इस घटना की चरम प्रकृति को अत्यधिक अप्रत्याशित माना जाता है, और यह ऐतिहासिक आंकड़ों को भी पार कर सकती है।"
बरसात का मौसम जल्दी समाप्त हो जाता है और गर्म मौसम जल्दी आ जाता है।
पिछले लगभग 40 वर्षों में दक्षिणी वियतनाम के मौसम के पैटर्न के विश्लेषण से पता चलता है कि अल नीनो की घटनाओं वाले वर्षों में आमतौर पर बारिश का मौसम पिछले वर्षों के औसत की तुलना में देर से शुरू होता है और जल्दी समाप्त होता है।
आपको यह भी पसंद आ सकता है
2026 में, दक्षिणी वियतनाम में बारिश का मौसम समय से पहले समाप्त होने का अनुमान है, लेकिन विभिन्न क्षेत्रों में इसमें भिन्नता देखने को मिलेगी।
पूर्वी क्षेत्र के उत्तरी भाग में, का माऊ और आन जियांग के तटों के किनारे, वर्षा ऋतु नवंबर के मध्य तक चल सकती है।
वहीं, पश्चिमी क्षेत्र के अंतर्देशीय इलाकों में, बारिश का मौसम अपेक्षाकृत जल्दी, लगभग मध्य से अक्टूबर के अंत तक समाप्त होने का अनुमान है।
दक्षिणी वियतनाम में कुल वार्षिक वर्षा, 2026 के अंतिम महीनों और 2027 की शुरुआत में होने वाली वर्षा, साथ ही वर्षा वाले दिनों की संख्या, सभी का पूर्वानुमान है कि यह कई वर्षों के औसत से काफी कम रहेगी।
मौसम पूर्वानुमानकर्ता किउ थी थुई ने यह भी कहा कि वर्षा की कमी के साथ-साथ, 2026-2027 की अवधि के दौरान दक्षिणी वियतनाम में तापमान कई वर्षों के औसत से काफी अधिक रहने का अनुमान है।
2026 के अंत तक स्थानीय स्तर पर भीषण गर्मी की लहरें आने की संभावना है, जो शुरू में पूर्वी प्रांतों में केंद्रित होंगी।
2027 की शुरुआत तक, लू की लहर पूरे क्षेत्र में तेजी से फैल जाएगी। ये लू की लहरें लंबी और तीव्र होने की संभावना है।
कई मौसम केंद्रों पर उच्चतम तापमान ऐतिहासिक रिकॉर्ड तक पहुंचने या उससे अधिक होने का खतरा है, जो 2015-2016 की अवधि के बराबर या उससे भी अधिक गंभीर हो सकता है।
मेकांग डेल्टा में भीषण सूखे और खारे पानी के घुसपैठ का खतरा बहुत अधिक है।
आपको यह भी पसंद आ सकता है
मौसम पूर्वानुमानकर्ता किउ थी थुई के अनुसार, व्यापक लू, बढ़ते तापमान और बारिश के मौसम के जल्दी समाप्त होने के कारण दक्षिणी वियतनाम में पानी की गंभीर कमी हो सकती है।
मौसम पूर्वानुमानकर्ता ने जोर देते हुए कहा, "मेकोंग डेल्टा (पश्चिमी क्षेत्र) में सूखे और खारे पानी के घुसपैठ की गंभीरता बेहद गंभीर होने का अनुमान है।"
इसके अलावा, 2027 की शुरुआत में पड़े सूखे के बाद, दक्षिणी वियतनाम में 2027 का वर्षा ऋतु भी कई वर्षों के औसत की तुलना में देरी से आने की संभावना है।
इसलिए, पूर्वानुमानकर्ताओं का कहना है कि इससे सूखा और खारेपन की स्थिति लंबी खिंच सकती है, साथ ही कृषि उत्पादन और लोगों की आजीविका पर काफी दबाव पड़ सकता है।

The greenest campaigners against climate change have long suffered from a crippling shortcoming: they too often frame the challenge as a problem of excess consumption. This motivates calls to “degrow” the economy and to curb the population. The claim is that humans consume too many resources, which in the context of climate change means too much energy.
Nowhere has the tension between this proposition and reality become more palpable during this sweltering summer than in the conversation over air conditioning.
If the atmosphere were to warm more than 3C above the average temperature in the preindustrial era, a prospect that looks ever more likely given the lackluster efforts to reduce carbon emissions, one in six of the world’s largest cities would suffer at least one heatwave per year lasting more than a month, according to the World Resources Institute. Low-income countries would suffer, on average, 6.9 heatwaves per year. Delhi would suffer at least 140 days with temperatures hitting at least 35C (95F).
Demand for AC around the world will inevitably accelerate as the atmosphere continues to warm. Ninety percent of households in the US and Japan enjoy artificial cooling. But in Indonesia, the share is only 9%. In India, it is 5%. Of the 2.8 billion people living in the hottest parts of the world, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA), only 8% currently possess AC. These countries are populous, they are generally poorer and they will get particularly hot as climate change progresses.
The global stock of air conditioners in buildings is expected to mushroom to 5.6bn by 2050, up from 2.5bn today, according to the IEA. In India alone, installed AC inventory will rise from 48m units in 2020 to 1.1bn in 2050, a 23-fold increase. Even if the world met the emissions targets laid out in the 2015 Paris climate accords – which is not going to happen – an average of 40% to 50% of the population in many of the world’s warmest countries would still require AC.
This is going to require a lot of energy. Scientists at Harvard’s School of Engineering and applied sciences estimated that in India and Indonesia, demand for power just for cooling in 2050 could be as high as 75% of their current total annual electricity demand.
This poses a challenge for the climate. In 2022, energy for cooling, mostly for residential and nonresidential space cooling but also to maintain cold chains for food and pharmaceutical production, and to cool transport, accounted for roughly 2.5bn tons of CO2 equivalent emissions, according to a United Nations report, about 7% of total emissions. In the absence of further strategies to improve energy efficiency and improve passive cooling techniques, it would rise to nearly 8bn tons by 2050.
So what does one do? Apparently, 58% of the French would rather “suffer from the heat than install an air conditioner in order to protect the environment”. But these sentiments cannot drive the world’s response to a warming world. To fight the battle against climate change requires, in fact, facilitating access to AC for billions of people who are now at risk of facing a hotter planet without the technology to protect themselves and their economies.
This proposition doesn’t rest only on arguments from ethics – although there are plenty of those. For starters, there is substantial evidence that air conditioning reduces heat’s impact on health. One study of US data found that the lethality of days hotter than 80F (27C) declined by about 75% from 1900 to 2004, almost entirely due to the adoption of residential air conditioning. Asking countries not to deploy AC is tantamount to accepting higher mortality.
Another powerful reason is that limiting access to air conditioning will set back economic growth. There is abundant evidence that excessive heat in the workplace reduces labor productivity and that air conditioning mitigates the decline. Heat can also stymie student achievement, eroding human capital.
Those living in India, Bangladesh, Indonesia or other unbearably hot places wherever will not heed the call to resist AC. Demanding unrealistic policies that are detrimental to their development is a straightforward strategy to ensure these countries do not cooperate with the effort to slow climate change. Campaigns from the west to stop hydropower in Africa, (even as westerners also called to stop developing fossil fuels on the continent) delivered little and engendered ill will. Trying to limit their access to AC would do the same.
Whether it is to power industries, improve transportation, or cool homes and workplaces, achieving faster economic growth will require poor hot countries around the world to consume more energy. Their economic development is indispensable for the global battle against climate change.
Just as fans of depopulation must understand that innovation needs people, fans of shrinking humanity’s footprint on the planet to prevent climate change misunderstand how humanity has prospered despite environmental constraints: through innovation. The path to decarbonization requires figuring out how to produce zero-carbon energy on a vast scale everywhere. It will be easier to do this in a rich world with AC and refrigeration than in a poor hot one.

After a brief reprieve from the heat, temperatures could reach almost 30C in parts of the UK due to a brief warm spell today.
Southern winds are set to bring hot and humid conditions back to England, with the hottest areas reaching 28C today.
The warm spell won’t last long, however – temperatures are expected to dip again later this week as rain and wind moves in.
From mid-September onwards, prediction of the weather is much less accurate.
The Met Office said: ‘As we head further into September, the distribution of rainfall becomes increasingly uncertain at this range. Settled or dry spells are still likely between weather systems.
‘Temperatures are likely to be around average overall, although some warm spells are possible, particularly in the south.’
WX Charts predicted that temperatures could reach 25C again by September 5 in southern England.
‘Intense’ thunderstorms and heavy rain across much of England and Wales could cause travel disruption this week, forecasters have warned.
After five heat waves this summer, Brits were relieved when bands of heavy showers and thunderstorms began moving in last week.
The UK is also bracing for a slew of storms and rainfall this autumn and winter brought by the pesky El Nino phenomenon.
El Nino happens every three to seven years when worldwide temperatures are pushed up by the weather system, which shifts ocean winds.
The natural warming of sea temperatures is forecast to reach more than 3°C in the coming months, making this year’s weather front ‘the largest since the 19th century,’ according to the Met Office forecasters.
‘We should be clear that this is an unprecedented event,’ Professor Adam Scaife, Met Office’s head of long range forecasting said.

By Danielle Cabugao
KUWAIT: Returning home from the sweltering heat, Safah Malik felt an inexplicable exhaustion and strange nausea. For months, her menstrual cycle had become increasingly unpredictable. She assumed the symptoms were hers alone, but stumbling upon conversations online, she discovered that women across the world were also experiencing intense symptoms, skipping periods, or experiencing them twice a month; the realization that her irregularities were part of a rising global crisis was “eye-opening.”
From June to July, concerned women—like Safah—have been searching for answers after sharing the same experience with their menstrual cycles this summer, which led to speculation about climate change and environmental exposures as causes of this weird phenomenon.
Online phenomenon debunked
Dr Nazha Bader AlFaraj, an OB-GYN resident from the Kuwaiti Board of Gynecologists, clarified that there is limited local evidence directly linking Kuwait’s weather to menstrual irregularity. She quickly debunks online speculations: “I wouldn’t call it a proven summer phenomenon. It’s probably less about the heat itself and more about the summer lifestyle: travel, late nights, stress, dehydration, diet changes, and exercise can all shift ovulation.” Hence, the sudden syncing of cycles is purely coincidental. She added: “There’s no evidence that everyone’s ovaries suddenly joined the same group chat.”
When the topic of a “universal sync” begins trending online, thousands of people who post about being late will gather up for discussion, while those who experienced normal cycles are excluded from the conversation. A fourth-year OB-GYN resident, Dr Farah Akbar, called the Internet discourse “anecdotal evidence.” However, both doctors acknowledged potential factors in Kuwait, like heatwaves and dust pollution, may contribute to the reports of delayed, missed or double periods.
Hormone and lifestyle disruptions
The two gynecologists observe no seasonal spikes in period concerns. Once a patient reports any irregular symptoms, obstetricians and gynecologists will delve into her lifestyle. Timing and patterns are sought out first. “If the cycle changes around the same time as major stress, travel, poor sleep, weight loss or gain, dieting, or intense exercise, lifestyle may be contributing,” said Dr AlFaraj.
For example, Dr Akbar points to women working late overnight shifts, which disrupts the body’s circadian rhythm. In combination with excessive sweating in the heat, menstruating women who work at irregular hours are more “sensitive,” which leads to an overall negative impact on reproductive cycles and endocrine health. Once medical causes are ruled out, the doctors begin considering the climate as a contributing factor.
Dr Akbar referenced research from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC): Being exposed to high heat for a long time is considered physiological stress can affect the menstrual cycle and hormonal health. Specifically, heat exposure increases the chances of fertility issues, while dehydration and excessive sweating can intensify cramps and pre-menstrual symptoms. She explains that the relationship between heat and hormones works both ways. “The extreme heat affects the woman’s hormones, and the hormones also affect the way that the woman can then tolerate the heat.”
Air pollution impact
Living in Kuwait’s dusty climate can also affect a woman’s body. Found in dust, particulate matter (PM) is a highly prominent air pollutant, along with other gases such as nitric oxide and sulfur oxides. Dr Akbar highlighted that these air pollutants are well-established endocrine disruptors, affecting the regulation of female hormones. This worsens fatigue, nausea and irregularity. To optimize hormonal health, women in Kuwait are advised to control their daily environments by staying in air-conditioned spaces to reduce physical and outdoor heat stress. “In terms of the air pollution, obviously there’s not much we can do there, but we can consider having an air purifier, which you can buy and keep in your homes, just to keep the air clear,” suggested Dr Akbar.
They advise women in Kuwait to proactively practice self-care during the summer, emphasizing hydration, regular sleep and non-rigorous exercise. “A slightly late period usually isn’t dramatic, but if your cycle completely loses the plot, get it checked,” reassured AlFaraj. She also considers Kuwait a great place for further studies correlating women’s health with climate change and air pollution. “There are a lot of factors we could look at beyond the temperature [...] I’d love to see local studies tracking women’s cycles alongside heat exposure, hydration, sleep, stress, exercise and hormonal conditions.”

Hong Kong open to classifying heatstroke as an occupational disease: labour chief
Commissioner for Labour Sam Hui also says revamped heat warning system would have triggered stronger alerts on two exceptionally hot days in August
Hong Kong authorities are open to classifying heatstroke as an occupational disease, the city’s labour chief has said, acknowledging that the recently revamped heat warning system would have triggered stronger alerts on two exceptionally hot days last month.
Commissioner for Labour Sam Hui Chark-shum said retrospective modelling showed the revised system would have issued a black warning on August 8 and a red alert on August 9, when the Observatory recorded 36.9 degrees Celsius (98.4 Fahrenheit) at its headquarters – the highest temperature since records began in 1884.
“If we had applied the revamped Heat Stress at Work Warning system, we would have issued a red warning on August 9 and even a black warning on August 8,” Hui told a television programme on Sunday.
The heat stress warning system has three levels – amber, red and black – and advises employers on rest arrangements for outdoor workers and those in indoor environments without air conditioning.
Amber signals significant heat stress and advises employers to arrange additional rest periods, while black is the highest warning level, under which workers performing heavy or very heavy labour should suspend work.

The Department of Meteorology has issued an amber warm weather advisory for several parts of the country, warning that the heat index could reach the Caution’ level during the daytime tomorrow (07).
The advisory, issued by the Natural Hazards Early Warning Centre at 4.00 p.m. today (06) will be in effect for residents of the North Central and Eastern provinces and the Jaffna, Kilinochchi, Mullaitivu, Vavuniya, Kurunegala, Monaragala and Hambantota districts.
The Department said the heat index — the temperature actually felt by the human body based on a combination of temperature and relative humidity — is expected to rise to cautionary levels at some locations.
Authorities have urged the general public to take precautions, particularly during the hottest parts of the day.
Meanwhile, those working at job sites have been advised to stay hydrated and take frequent breaks in shaded areas, while strenuous outdoor activities should be limited where possible.
The Department has also urged the public to check on elderly and sick persons, while motorists have been reminded never to leave children unattended inside vehicles.
The general public is further advised to seek shade, drink sufficient water and wear lightweight, white or light-coloured clothing to reduce the effects of the heat.
